William Klapp Williams wrote this Johns Hopkins University study in 1891, as numbers five and six of the ninth series on historical and political science, edited by Herbert B. Adams. Williams, of the Newberry Library in Chicago, asks how Lombard towns grew into self-governing communes.

Part one traces the Lombard conquest and its aftermath from the sixth century, weighing Roman municipal survival against Germanic custom, bishops power, and trade. Later parts follow the communes to the tenth century, seeking the causes of municipal unity. The study is dry and documentary, built on charters and chronicles, and it shows American graduate scholarship of its day at work on a European problem: how cities learned to rule themselves.

Marvin Warshay at Lewis Research Center wrote this May 1965 symposium paper on cleaning up a difficult measurement. A shock tube blasts a gas with a sudden pressure wave, heating it in an instant. In that heat, bromine molecules fall apart, or dissociate. Noble gases mixed with the bromine form the setting for the rate study. Small errors can badly skew the measured rates.

Warshay works through where the errors enter and how to keep them small. Rate data feed the chemistry used in engines and reentry work. A symposium on shock tubes gave specialists a place to compare such methods. His paper is a methods piece, valued less for a single number than for making later numbers more trustworthy.

Herbert G. Hurrell, Fred Boecker Jr., and Kent S. Jefferies of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a 1970 energy conversion conference in Las Vegas. It reports startup testing of the SNAP-8 power conversion system. SNAP-8 was a nuclear power system built around a mercury working loop.

Bringing such a loop to life takes careful control gear. The team notes that some startup controls and equipment were not flight-type parts. A gas-pressurized reservoir served to inject the working fluid at startup. Tests of this kind showed whether the power system could be started in a safe, repeatable way.
nasa-tm-19720016560-iterative-computatio:
James W Steincamp of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this computing paper on December 7, 1971, as NASA TM X-64654. He worked in Program Development there. The paper tackles the generalized inverse of a matrix, a tool for solving awkward equation sets. Steincamp developed a step by step method that converges very fast. Each pass roughly cubes the accuracy of the last. A spacecraft steering problem gave the method its test case.

The paper supplies a working FORTRAN subroutine for the method. It handles real matrices on the CDC 3200 computer. A numerical example shows the accuracy reached in practice. The application computes steering laws for control moment gyroscopes. Those spinning wheels turn spacecraft without using fuel. Fast, exact matrix tools made their control laws practical.

William Klapp Williams, Ph.D., wrote this investigation of the Lombard communes for the Johns Hopkins University Studies in Historical and Political Science. Herbert B. Adams edited the series, and this study appeared at Chicago in May and June 1891 as numbers five and six of the ninth series. Its question is how municipal unity grew among the Lombard communes between the sixth and tenth centuries.

Part I treats the Lombard conquest and its results. Williams starts from the land and its people, asking what made renewed town life possible at all. Local independence, he argues, grew from those conditions as a natural expression. The inquiry therefore starts with the first Lombard domination of the country. A motto from Rothari's laws stands at the head, and a Freeman line frames the series: history is past politics, and politics present history.
